title: Does an Executable Generate–Validate–Repair Loop Reduce Semantic Failures in LLM-Generated NetOps Changes?
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that tested whether inserting an executable emulator validator into a generate→validate→repair pipeline (guarded) reduces semantic/network-level failures versus an LLM-only suggestion workflow (baseline). The experiment used a deterministic paired design with N=120 intent→configuration tasks (40 tasks per topology class: edge, core, leaf–spine). A single shared initial candidate was produced per task by gpt-5-mini (model_calls_used = 120) and evaluated under both conditions. A deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) performed full intent-constraint and workflow-policy checks and could trigger at most one repair iteration per guarded episode. Outcomes: baseline success = 120/120; guarded success = 120/120; contingency: n_11=120, n_10=0, n_01=0, n_00=0. Exact two-sided McNemar p = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00; bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Validator traces show repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes. We incorporate artifact-grounded clarifications of shared-generation semantics, repair-trigger logic, and the statistical degeneracy observed; expand methodological detail, execution accounting, representative diagnostics, and reproducibility guidance; and discuss construct and external validity limits grounded in the archived run artifacts.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into network configuration commands, promising efficiency gains for NetOps. However, syntactically plausible commands can violate workflow invariants (for example, changing MTU without an enforced shutdown or performing a hazardous uplink switchover), cause regressions, or otherwise produce semantic failures not visible from text-only checks. Prior proposals therefore recommend integrating verification, emulation, digital twins, or veto layers so generated candidates are validated before enactment. Evaluating these guarded pipelines requires closed-loop executable tests that detect semantic/network-level errors beyond token- or syntax-level correctness.

We designed a preregistered paired experiment to isolate whether an executable validator (and a single-step repair policy) can reduce semantic failures when the same generator output is presented to both a baseline (LLM-only) and a guarded (generate→validate→repair) workflow. Our confirmatory research question (registered as CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) was: Does integrating an executable network emulator as a validator in a generate→validate→repair pipeline reduce semantic/network-level failures when enacting LLM-generated configuration changes compared to an LLM-only suggestion workflow? To isolate validator/repair effects we used a shared-initial-candidate paired design: for each task the same generated candidate was evaluated by both conditions. This isolates the marginal effect of the validator/repair stage on identical generator outputs and avoids conflation with generator variability.

Contributions. (1) A preregistered, artifact-rich paired experiment (N=120 pairs) that holds the generator fixed and measures the incremental effect of an executable validator plus bounded repair on emulator-observed semantic failures; (2) exact execution accounting and deterministic reconciliation demonstrating completion of the preregistered protocol (planned and completed episodes, model-call counts, contamination checks, and scorer/validator traces); (3) an artifact-grounded analysis and interpretation of a degenerate ceiling outcome (100% success in both conditions), including explicit bootstrap and McNemar reporting; and (4) methodological recommendations for future confirmatory designs when generators produce fewer valid candidates.
sections.related_work:
Recent work highlights the limits of text-only evaluation for NetOps tasks and emphasizes executable closed-loop benchmarks, emulation, and verification as necessary to reveal operational failure modes (see NetConfArena and other executable testbeds). Prior empirical and survey studies report that generate→validate→repair patterns, tool-augmented agent architectures, and veto/guardrail layers reduce semantic errors in constrained scenarios. Surveys and tool papers also document guardrail proposals (canaries, veto layers, model→formal-model translations) intended to improve operational safety.

Our study is motivated by and complements these prior efforts by holding the generator fixed and focusing on whether an external validator/repair stage can change outcomes for identical generated candidates. This isolates a mechanistic question distinct from prior work that aggregates generator and verifier effects across heterogeneous stacks. The literature also identifies open gaps that influenced our preregistered exploratory plan: scarcity of production-rooted incident corpora with verifiable ground truth, limited cross-model comparisons under identical executable harnesses, and under-explored uncertainty calibration methods for structured configuration outputs. We adopt a deterministic, artifact-forward design to enable future reuse and direct comparison against the archived task bank and validator.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design. The study was preregistered as CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1 and archived prior to execution. The preregistration specified a paired-binary design with exactly N=120 distinct intent→configuration tasks, deterministically assigned into three topology classes (edge/core/leaf–spine) with 40 tasks each. Each task produced one shared initial candidate generated by the declared hosted model (gpt-5-mini) and used by both conditions (independent_condition_generation=false). A guarded repair could be invoked at most once and only when the deterministic emulator validator reported validator.violation_count>0.

Task corpus and task metadata. Tasks were produced by a deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) and include explicit machine-readable payloads: initial_state, expected_final_state, intent, and a required_sequence that encodes the correct command order (examples: shut→mtu→vlan→up, make-before-break sequences, or group-availability constraints). Each manifest entry includes difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, required_command_count, and an explicit difficulty level) to support stratified analyses.

Generation stage and shared-candidate semantics. The single shared candidate per pair was produced by the declared gpt-5-mini configuration (execution/model_configuration.json). The execution manifest records model_calls_used = 120 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 120}. This shared-generation design isolates the validator/repair marginal effect by ensuring generator output is identical across baseline and guarded episodes for a given pair; i.e., the difference (if any) arises only from the validator and repair steps rather than from generation variability.

Validator and repair. The guarded pipeline used a deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, version 5.0) that executes intent-constraint and workflow-policy checks encoded in the task payload (for example, must_be_down_for_fields, final_group_constraints, make-before-break patterns). The validator emits a structured validator_trace including validation_before and validation_after states, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_count, and repair_applied. The preregistered repair policy invoked at most one repair iteration per guarded episode and only when validator.violation_count>0. Repair prompts and repair_provider_trace artifacts are archived when produced; none were produced in this run because violation_count=0 for every guarded episode.

Confirmatory estimand and statistical plan. The primary estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (per-pair reduction in emulator-observed semantic-failure probability). The prespecified confirmatory test was the exact two-sided McNemar. Complementary reporting included the paired-difference point estimate and a bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval computed with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). The preregistration specified a complete-pair primary analysis; technical/instrumentation failures would be excluded and logged, with a sensitivity analysis treating excluded items as failures. The preregistered power target was an absolute reduction of 0.15 with N=120 under plausible discordant-pair assumptions.

Instrumentation and contamination controls. The harness enforced deterministic emulator-state resets (container image checksum + deterministic seed) between tasks and recorded provider-call audit logs. Contamination heuristics (duplicate-output detection, cross-condition cache-key reuse) were applied; none triggered exclusions. All provider traces, responses, and scoring JSONs were archived together with an execution manifest and artifact hash manifest for reproducible verification.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The run completed the preregistered protocol. Planned_episode_count = 240; completed_episode_count = 240; model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). analysis/condition_summary.csv records baseline = 120 successes, 0 failures and guarded = 120 successes, 0 failures (success rates = 1.0 for both). analysis/missingness_summary.csv reports complete_pairs = 120 and zero technical/instrumentation exclusions; analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty.

Primary confirmatory outcome. The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) records n_11 = 120 (both conditions success), n_10 = 0 (guarded only), n_01 = 0 (baseline only), n_00 = 0 (both fail). With zero discordant pairs the exact two-sided McNemar p-value equals 1.0. The paired-difference point estimate is 0.00. The preregistered bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729) returned [0.00, 0.00]; the interval is degenerate because resampling an empirical table with no discordant pairs reproduces identical paired outcomes across resamples.

Per-topology breakdown. Tasks were deterministically partitioned with 40 tasks per topology class. Per-topology archived counts are:
- Edge (40 tasks): baseline successes = 40/40; guarded successes = 40/40.
- Core (40 tasks): baseline successes = 40/40; guarded successes = 40/40.
- Leaf–spine (40 tasks): baseline successes = 40/40; guarded successes = 40/40.
These counts are supported by execution/task_manifest.jsonl entries and the scoring JSONs in execution/scoring/.

Representative validator diagnostics. Representative scoring artifacts (for example, execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json and execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json) show: normalized_response equals normalized_reference_answer; parsed_command_count equals required_command_count listed in the task payload; validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true; validator_trace.repair_applied = false; validator_id = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; validator_version = 5.0. Example task payloads include required_sequence fields that the validator enforces (seen in the representative task-manifest entries). The absence of violations across examples documents that the generator produced sequences that satisfied encoded workflow policies for this task corpus and prompting configuration.

Repair activity and secondary endpoints. Because validator.violation_count = 0 for every guarded episode, repair_applied = false across the archive and no repair_provider_trace artifacts exist. Consequently, preregistered secondary endpoints (proportion of tasks requiring repair, mean repair calls per successful task) are vacuous for this run and are reported as such in the archived analysis artifacts.

Contamination and deterministic reconciliation. The deterministic_reconciliation.json artifact confirms complete accounting consistency (n_11=120, n_10=0, n_01=0, n_00=0), provider_call_audit showing hosted_model_call_event_count = 120, and no cross-condition cache reuse. No preregistered deviations or exclusions were logged.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation of the ceiling outcome. The shared-generation paired design was chosen to answer a narrowly scoped mechanistic question: can a validator/repair subsystem improve outcomes for identical generator outputs? In this archived task bank and under the declared generator/prompt configuration the shared initial candidates satisfied the deterministic emulator validator in all 120 pairs; consequently the guarded pipeline had no opportunity to exercise repair behavior and could not reduce semantic failures relative to the baseline. The observed exact McNemar p = 1.0 and bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00] are statistical expressions of this ceiling.

Methodological implications. A paired shared-generation design cleanly isolates validator/repair marginal effects but can hide repair utility if the generator produces very few invalid candidates on the chosen task corpus. This outcome demonstrates a trade-off: shared-generation reduces generator-induced variance (improving internal validity for the validator effect) but reduces external generalizability to settings where generator outputs vary or are noisier. For confirmatory tests intended to measure practical repair utility we recommend designs that allow independent per-condition generation (so that the guard can act on generator errors arising under realistic prompting variability), or deliberate prompt perturbations that increase generator error incidence while preserving other controls.

Threats to validity. Internal validity is supported by deterministic provisioning, exhaustive provider-call audit logs, zero exclusions, and reproducible validator traces. Construct validity is limited by the validator's encoding of workflow policies derived from the synthetic task payloads: these policies are explicit and reproducible but simplify real-world vendor heterogeneity, partial observability, and telemetry delays. External validity is constrained by the synthetic deterministic task corpus and single hosted model (gpt-5-mini). Conclusion validity is affected by the ceiling: the preregistered power calculation assumed a baseline failure rate near 0.40 and a target absolute reduction of 0.15; with baseline = 0.00 observed here those assumptions no longer apply and the confirmatory test is uninformative for the originally targeted effect size.

Operational implications. Even when unused, a deterministic validator that emits structured traces (what rules were checked, which fields were touched, and why a repair was not applied) supports operator auditability and post-hoc analysis. The archived artifacts show end-to-end instrumented accounting that can serve as a template for operator-facing explanations and independent audits. In deployments where generators occasionally produce invalid candidates, a generate→validate→repair pipeline with clear repair budgets and auditable traces remains a recommended architectural element.

Design recommendations for future studies. (1) Allow per-condition independent generation or introduce controlled prompt perturbations to increase the rate of generator-produced invalid candidates so that the guard can be exercised; (2) expand the repair budget to permit multi-iteration repair sequences and archive repair traces; (3) test multiple generator families and prompt strategies under the same executable harness to quantify cross-model generality; (4) use richer emulator models or multi-vendor behavioral models to increase construct realism; and (5) assemble or partner for production-rooted incident corpora with verifiable ground truth to improve external validity. The archived task_manifest includes difficulty metadata (dependency_rule_count, required_command_count, difficulty level) to support stratified follow-on comparisons.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=120) comparing an executable generate→validate→repair pipeline against an LLM-only workflow under a deterministic harness and a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini). All 120 shared initial candidates passed the deterministic emulator validator, producing n_11=120 (both conditions success) and a paired-difference estimate of 0.00 (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00], 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). The result documents a ceiling on this curated synthetic task bank and clarifies that a shared-generation paired design can mask repair benefits that would appear if generators sometimes produce invalid candidates. Our principal scientific contribution is methodological: we demonstrate how a preregistered, artifact-rich paired design cleanly isolates validator/repair effects and how deterministic archival artifacts (task manifests, validator traces, provider-call audits, and reconciliation files) enable reproducible failure analysis and transparent auditing even when the primary confirmatory test is degenerate. The archived artifacts and manifest permit follow-up studies that relax the shared-generation constraint, compare generator families, expand repair budgets, and evaluate more production-rooted corpora to quantify practical repair utility under realistic generator variance.

limitations: Confirmatory scope: results are narrowly scoped to the preregistered synthetic task set, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy; generalization to production heterogeneity is limited.
Synthetic task provenance: tasks were synthetic/deterministic and may underrepresent noisy, adversarial, or multi-vendor production incidents; external validity to live networks is constrained.

Shared-generation design: using a single shared initial generation per paired task isolates validator/repair efficacy but precludes detection of generation-variance effects; this choice contributed to the ceiling outcome and limits inference about repair utility on independently generated invalid outputs.

Validator fidelity: the deterministic emulator/validator is reproducible but simplifies heterogeneity present in multi-vendor, partially observable production environments; some real-world failure modes may not be exposed.

Statistical ceiling: baseline success reached 100% on the tested task bank, violating the preregistered power assumptions (targeted absolute reduction = 0.15) and rendering the McNemar confirmatory test uninformative for demonstrating the preregistered effect size.
